name: Translating Between Disciplines
title: Translating Between Disciplines
answer: Translating between disciplines is the work of moving a finding, method or term from the field that produced it into another field that can use it, without losing what it meant in the original. In evidence synthesis it covers everything from reading a clinical trial through an economics lens to restating a machine learning result for a policy audience. The scope includes vocabulary, study design, statistical conventions and the standards each field treats as proof. It is not a single technique but a set of habits that sit between literature review and writing.

sections.body: Translating between disciplines is the work of moving a finding, method or term from the field that produced it into another field that can use it, without losing what it meant in the original. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on access to primary sources, so a translator needs the original paper rather than a summary of it, which is why this site links to the original paper and never to the Consensus search tool.Reference managers, citation databases and shared ontologies carry the rest of the load.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with locating the claim in its home discipline and recording the study design, the population and the measure that produced it. The translator then maps each term to its nearest equivalent in the target field and states plainly where no equivalent exists. Claims are extracted and compared across sources rather than taken one at a time, which is how 14104 claims from research works become usable as a body rather than a pile. A written note on what was changed in translation, and why, is part of the output, not an afterthought.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and provenance decide whether a translation can be published at all, since a restated finding still belongs to the paper it came from. Attribution must survive the move, and a translated claim that cannot be traced back to its source should not be circulated. Where a discipline's conventions differ on consent, data sharing or authorship, the stricter convention usually governs the joint work. Reviewers should be able to see the original wording beside the translated wording, and any change in strength of evidence should be flagged rather than smoothed over.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward shared vocabularies and machine assisted mapping, with glossaries and claim databases doing more of the matching work.The harder problem is not finding an equivalent word but preserving the strength of the original evidence through the move. Expect translation to become a named step in review protocols rather than an informal courtesy between co authors.
